body_markdown:
*Tom* writes:


Our 1998 Mercedes-Benz C230 has an electrical issue that sometimes causes the windows to open overnight, the doors not to lock or unlock, the windows not to close, the ABS light to come on, and the cruise control not to work. It’s all intermittent.


If I disconnect and reconnect the battery, everything will work well for a few days. I can’t find anyone with a scanner that will work on this vehicle.


Otherwise, the drivetrain is great, and the vehicle is a comfortable ride. Any suggestions? Thanks!


*Sajeev* answers:


I hate to say it, but you really need to find someone with that scanner. The other option is inserting yourself into the diagnostic tree, but I am getting ahead of myself.


The Mercedes’ computer needs to have a little chat with a diagnostic tool, *and that’s that.* I could say you have a bad battery, a corroded/pinched/broken wiring harness in need of repair, or a bad CCM (Convenience Control Module). But this is certainly[not the time to fire the parts cannon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/advice/piston-slap/piston-slap-fire-the-parts-cannon/) and hope for the best.


So here’s one option: Take a page from my book, and buy the tools and repair/training manuals to do part of the complex electrical diagnoses on your own. I am by no means a master technician, but I have narrowed down problems far enough that a professional mechanic (who would prefer to work on a newer, easier-to-fix vehicle) becomes willing to take it to the finish line.


But your situation is different, as my vehicles (1980s-90s Lincoln-Mercury products) are often diagnosed with a[paper clip and a forum posting](https://www.ford-trucks.com/forums/1715941-how-to-retrieve-trouble-codes-from-fords-eec-iv-with-a-paper-clip.html) . Your Mercedes’ 38-pin diagnostic system requires a bespoke scan tool that costs more than a paper clip, but at least there are[plenty of options](https://www.google.com/search?sca_esv=d7bb3ee0c0ddd2fe&rlz=1C5GCCM_en&sxsrf=APpeQnv0EqvCCOR5XcwSWMV3-0NkI2QJLw:1787251953980&udm=28&fbs=ABfTbFVyMZGZf1hfvX9uKjN_-G8cqCQj_06QnZs315LoFmPf5bBLHMJ0vMQmTbuI72DM7jnxvATrUU2Yg9dwuUGnsUHcXPuOM0_k1dPPnMiKJgy16dZbzxEzLfw8wuRMswCXrs8RnrM5_piPyuLg1-_LQAE92ad1fZ-qK1FCpvbuQCj2oVGAmluL385MBmH-GXGJSIp0KmSpSJ5ZouKtlsdTwkrdl0Legg&q=38+pin+mercedes+diagnostic+scanner&ved=1t:220175&ictx=111&biw=1280&bih=588&dpr=2&safe=active&ssui=on) out there. Do your homework, though, and confirm with a forum or an independent mechanic which tool is preferred for your vehicle. My colleague, Eddy Eckart, tried a couple of tools on his of-the-same-era Porsche Boxster and they did not have the functionality claimed in the ads.


Alongside a Mercedes-specific scan tool, you also need factory Mercedes-Benz repair manuals or an online equivalent. I recommend the books so you can share them with any shop to help repair your vehicle, not to turn yourself into a Mercedes-Benz technician in your spare time.


But you should get a basic idea of how the tool works, what codes it generates, and how to use the book to help narrow down the problem. By doing this, you insert yourself into the diagnostic tree when repairing your car. Let’s face it, you are in the same boat as yours truly: nobody wants to work on an obscure old luxury car. If you can’t find a shop willing to work with you, there are likely only two choices: become part of the diagnostic tree, or sell the car and buy something with more readily available technical support. I have done the first of those choices, and it’s been a smashing success!


I feel like I am being harsh or dismissive of other options, but this is the same crossroads I faced over 20 years ago with my Lincolns. It worked out for me, as it turned into a *Piston Slappin’ career* , but I became hands-on simply for the love of my vehicles.


I fear you are at that crossroads, and the choice is in your hands. There’s no wrong answer, unless someone in the comments below offers a solution I never considered. So tell us, dear reader, what should Tom do about the electrical problems on his 1998 Mercedes C-Class?
